part.title: Verbs
part.description: The six verb types, consonant gradation in verbs, the imperative and useful verb patterns.

topics.title: The six verb types — overview
topics.summary: Every Finnish verb belongs to one of six types, recognised from the end of the infinitive. The type tells you how to find the stem.

sections.heading: Personal endings are the same for every verb
sections.body: What differs between the types is only **how you get the stem** from the infinitive.

sections.heading: How to recognise the type
sections.tip: Check the **last two letters** first: -da/-dä → type 2; double consonant or -st- + a → type 3; vowel + a → type 1; t + a after a vowel → 4, 5 or 6 (look at the vowel before -ta).

sections.heading: Which types have K-P-T?
bullets: **Type 1**: infinitive is strong → minä, sinä, me, te and the negative are **weak** (*nukkua → nukun*). See [[kpt-verbs|K-P-T in verb type 1]].
**Types 3 and 4** (and 6): infinitive is **weak** → all personal forms are **strong** (*ajatella → ajattelen*, *tavata → tapaan*). See [[kpt-verbs-3-4|K-P-T in types 3 & 4]].

sections.heading: Exceptions worth knowing
bullets: **olla** (to be) — olen, olet, on, olemme, olette, ovat.
**tehdä** (to do/make) — teen, teet, tekee, teemme, teette, tekevät.
**nähdä** (to see) — näen, näet, näkee, näemme, näette, näkevät.
Some -ita/-eta verbs belong to type 4: **hävitä** → häviän, **kiivetä** → kiipeän, **selvitä** → selviän.

topics.title: Verb type 1 (-a/-ä after a vowel)
topics.summary: The biggest group: puhua, asua, ostaa, lukea… Drop the final -a/-ä to get the stem; hän doubles the last vowel.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Infinitive minus the final **-a/-ä** = stem. Add the personal endings. In the **hän** form the last vowel of the stem doubles (unless it is already long or a diphthong ending in the same vowel).
sections.note: *lukea* shows K-P-T: k disappears in the weak forms (luen, luet). See [[kpt-verbs|K-P-T in verb type 1]].

sections.heading: Common type 1 verbs from the course

examples.en: I live in London and speak English.

examples.fi: Mitä tämä maksaa? — Se maksaa kaksi euroa.
examples.en: How much does this cost? — It costs two euros.
The children are playing in the yard.
We're watching a film in the evening.

topics.title: K-P-T in verb type 1
topics.summary: nukkua → minä nukun, hän nukkuu. In type 1, minä/sinä/me/te and the negative take the weak grade; hän and he stay strong.

sections.heading: The pattern
sections.body: The endings **-n, -t, -mme, -tte** close the syllable → **weak grade**. The hän form (long vowel) and he form (-vat) keep it open → **strong grade**. The negative uses the same stem as minä → **weak**.

sections.heading: All the changes

rows: ottaa, odottaa, kirjoittaa, soittaa, auttaa, muuttaa

sections.note: No gradation after s, or in st, sk, tk, ts: *istua → istun*, *etsiä → etsin*, *tutkia → tutkin*, *katsoa → katson*.

examples.en: I usually sleep eight hours.

examples.fi: Hän lukee kirjaa, mutta minä en lue.
examples.en: He/she is reading a book, but I'm not.
We leave for the cottage on Friday.

examples.fi: Pidän kahvista, mutta en pidä teestä.
examples.en: I like coffee, but I don't like tea.

examples.fi: Tiedätkö, missä asema on? — En tiedä.
examples.en: Do you know where the station is? — I don't know.

topics.title: Verb type 2 (-da/-dä)
topics.summary: syödä, juoda, käydä, tehdä, nähdä… Drop -da/-dä; the hän form is just the stem. No consonant gradation (except tehdä/nähdä).

sections.heading: Formation
bullets: **tehdä** and **nähdä** are irregular: stem *tee-/näe-*, but *tekee/näkee* and *tekevät/näkevät*.

examples.fi: Syön aamulla puuroa ja juon kahvia.
examples.en: In the morning I eat porridge and drink coffee.
I go to the shop every day.
What are you doing at the weekend?
Can I help? — May I have some coffee?

topics.title: Verb type 3 (-la, -na, -ra, -sta)
topics.summary: tulla → tulen, mennä → menen, nousta → nousen, opiskella → opiskelen. Drop the last two letters and add -e.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Remove the last two letters (**-la/-lä, -na/-nä, -ra/-rä, -ta/-tä**) and add **-e**. hän lengthens it: **-ee**.
sections.note: **juosta** (run) is irregular: *juoksen, juokset, juoksee*. **olla** is technically type 3 but irregular.

examples.en: Are you coming tomorrow? — Yes.
I'm going home by bus.
In winter we skate and ski.
He/she studies Finnish on Mondays.

sections.heading: Reverse K-P-T
sections.body: Some type 3 verbs have a weak grade in the infinitive and a strong grade in all personal forms: *ajatella → ajattelen*, *kuunnella → kuuntelen*. See [[kpt-verbs-3-4|K-P-T in verb types 3 & 4]].

topics.title: Verb type 4 (-ata, -ota, -uta, -ätä…)
topics.summary: haluta → haluan, avata → avaan, pelata → pelaan. Drop -ta and add -a/-ä.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Remove **-ta/-tä** and add **-a/-ä** (so -ata becomes -aa-, -uta becomes -ua-). hän adds another vowel unless there are already two the same (*avaa*, but *haluaa*).

examples.en: Would you like some coffee? — Yes, I would.
The shop opens at nine o'clock.
In winter we play ice hockey.
Can you swim? — Yes, I can.
I wake up at seven o'clock.

sections.heading: Reverse K-P-T
sections.body: When the infinitive has a weak consonant, **every** personal form (including hän and he) is strong: *tavata → tapaan, tapaa, tapaavat*; *pakata → pakkaan*; *hypätä → hyppään*. See [[kpt-verbs-3-4|K-P-T in verb types 3 & 4]].

topics.title: Verb type 5 (-ita/-itä)
topics.summary: tarvita → tarvitsen, valita → valitsen. Drop -a/-ä and add -se.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Remove the final **-a/-ä** and add **-se**; hän: **-see**. No consonant gradation.
sections.note: A few -ita/-itä verbs are actually type 4: *hävitä → häviän* (lose), *selvitä → selviän* (survive), *levitä → leviän* (spread).

examples.en: I need new shoes.
In winter we need warm clothes.
What does this word mean?
Will you choose coffee or tea?

topics.title: Verb type 6 (-eta/-etä)
topics.summary: A small group meaning 'to become …': vanheta → vanhenen (grow old), lämmetä → lämpenee (get warmer).

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Remove **-ta/-tä** and add **-ne**; hän: **-nee**. Reverse K-P-T like types 3 and 4 (*lämmetä → lämpenee*).

examples.fi: Syksyllä ilma kylmenee ja illat pimenevät.
examples.en: In autumn the air gets colder and the evenings get darker.
In spring the weather gets warmer.

topics.title: K-P-T in verb types 3 & 4
topics.summary: Reverse gradation: the infinitive is weak, every personal form is strong — tavata → tapaan, tapaa; ajatella → ajattelen, ajattelee.

sections.heading: Why it's 'reverse'
sections.body: In types 3 and 4 the infinitive ends in a closed syllable (*a-ja-tel-la*, *ta-vat-a*), so the infinitive has the **weak** grade. In the personal forms the syllable is open (*a-jat-te-len*, *ta-paan*), so they have the **strong** grade. And because the ending doesn't close anything new, **all six persons and the negative are strong** — unlike type 1, where hän/he differ.

sections.heading: All the changes (weak → strong)

rows: pakata → pakkaan, hakata → hakkaan, leikata → leikkaan
mitata → mittaan, ajatella → ajattelen, jutella → juttelen, esitellä → esittelen, luetella → luettelen
pudota → putoan, kadota → katoan, riidellä → riitelen
tavata → tapaan, luvata → lupaan, kaivata → kaipaan, levätä → lepään

sections.note: Not every v or l alternates: *avata → avaan*, *kävellä → kävelen*, *pelata → pelaan* have no gradation. Watch out for st, sk: *opiskella → opiskelen*, *vastata → vastaan*.

examples.en: I'm meeting my friend at the café.
I'll pack my bag in the evening.

examples.fi: Hän kuuntelee musiikkia ja ajattelee kesää.
examples.en: He/she listens to music and thinks about summer.
The leaves fall from the trees in autumn.
The children jump and run in the yard.

topics.title: Imperative — giving instructions
topics.summary: Tule! (Come!) — Tulkaa! (Come, all of you!) — Älä tule! — Älkää tulko! The singular imperative looks like the minä form without -n.

sections.heading: Singular (to one person, sinä)
sections.body: Take the **minä** form and drop **-n**. It is the same as the negative stem, so K-P-T type 1 verbs are **weak**: *nukkua → nuku!*

sections.heading: Plural / polite (to several people, te)
sections.body: Take the **infinitive stem** (type 1 & 2: drop -a/-ä or -da/-dä; types 3–5: drop only the last vowel) and add **-kaa/-kää**. Negative: **älkää** + stem + **-ko/-kö**. Type 1 keeps the **strong** grade.
sections.tip: Shortcut for types 3, 4 and 5: infinitive minus final -a/-ä + kaa: *tulla → tul(l) → tulkaa*, *avata → avat + kaa*.

sections.heading: Let's …! (me)
sections.body: In spoken Finnish 'let's' is the passive form: **Mennään!** (Let's go!), **Syödään!** (Let's eat!), **Aloitetaan!** (Let's start!). Negative: *Ei mennä!*

sections.heading: The object of an imperative
sections.body: A whole, countable object is in the **basic form** (no -n): *Osta leipä!* (Buy a loaf!), *Avaa ovi!* (Open the door!). Uncountable or negative → partitive: *Osta maitoa! Älä avaa ovea!*

examples.en: Listen! Repeat! Write! (to the class)
Open your books at page ten.

examples.fi: Istu alas! Ole hyvä ja istu.
examples.en: Sit down! Please sit down.

examples.fi: Hengitä sisään… ja ulos. Nosta kädet ylös.
examples.en: Breathe in… and out. Raise your arms. (yoga)
Turn right and go straight on.
Don't forget the keys!
Come here! Wait a moment!

topics.title: Verb patterns: I want to…, I like…
topics.summary: Haluan syödä (I want to eat), Osaan uida (I can swim), Pidän kahvista (I like coffee), Tykkään hiihtää.

sections.heading: Verb + infinitive
sections.body: Many verbs are followed by a second verb in the **infinitive** (dictionary form):

rows: Haluan oppia suomea. — I want to learn Finnish.
Voin tulla huomenna. — I can come tomorrow.
Saanko istua tässä? — May I sit here?
Alkaa sataa. — It's starting to rain.
Yritän puhua suomea. — I try to speak Finnish.
Minun täytyy mennä. — I have to go.

sections.heading: Liking: pitää + elative (-sta/-stä)
sections.body: **pitää** ('to like') takes its object in the **elative**: *pidän kahvista* = I like coffee. (In speech, **tykätä** works the same way: *tykkään kahvista*.)

examples.fi: Pidän suklaasta, mutta en pidä lakritsista.
examples.en: I like chocolate, but I don't like liquorice.

examples.fi: Mistä sinä pidät? — Pidän joogasta ja kävelystä.
examples.en: What do you like? — I like yoga and walking.
Do you like sauna?
